format: Text with inline TeX in $...$ and display TeX in $$...$$. Answer label and value fields are TeX without delimiters.

problems.title: EMF in a stationary coil
problems.prompt: A 10-turn coil of area $0.05\ \mathrm{m^2}$ sits in $\mathbf{B}=\hat{\mathbf{z}}\,0.1\cos(120\pi t)\ \mathrm{T}$, with its normal along $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$. Find the induced EMF.

problems.title: Sliding bar on rails
problems.prompt: A metal bar $0.5\ \mathrm{m}$ long slides at $4\ \mathrm{m/s}$ along rails in a uniform $0.3\ \mathrm{T}$ field normal to the rails. The circuit resistance is $2\ \Omega$. Find the EMF, the current, the force needed to keep the bar moving, and the power.
hints: The current in the bar feels $F=I\ell B$, opposing the motion (Lenz).
steps: The mechanical power you supply equals the electrical power dissipated in the resistor.

problems.title: A simple generator
problems.prompt: A 100-turn coil of area $100\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ spins at $60$ revolutions per second in a uniform $0.5\ \mathrm{T}$ field. Find the peak and RMS EMF.

problems.title: Which way does the current flow?
problems.prompt: A horizontal wire loop sits in a vertical magnetic field pointing up, and the field is getting stronger. Looking down from above, which way does the induced current flow? What if the field is getting weaker?
hints: The induced current makes a field that opposes the change.
Use the right-hand rule: counterclockwise current (seen from above) makes a field pointing up.
steps: The upward flux is increasing, so the induced field must point down inside the loop.
A downward field inside the loop needs clockwise current, seen from above.
If the field is weakening, the induced field points up to prop up the flux: counterclockwise.

problems.title: Ideal transformer
problems.prompt: An ideal transformer has $100$ primary turns and $500$ secondary turns. With $10\ \mathrm{V}$ RMS on the primary and a $250\ \Omega$ load, find the secondary voltage and both currents.
hints: The same flux links both coils, so the voltage per turn is the same.
steps: Power in, $10\times1=10$ W, equals power out, $50\times0.2=10$ W.

problems.title: Displacement current density
problems.prompt: In a lossless dielectric with $\varepsilon_r=4$, $\mathbf{E}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}\,100\cos(10^9t)\ \mathrm{V/m}$. Find $\mathbf{J}_d$.

problems.title: Is seawater a conductor?
problems.prompt: Seawater has $\sigma=4\ \mathrm{S/m}$ and $\varepsilon_r=81$. Find $\sigma/(\omega\varepsilon)$ at $1\ \mathrm{MHz}$ and at $10\ \mathrm{GHz}$, and the frequency where conduction and displacement currents are equal.
steps: Seawater is a good conductor at 1 MHz but behaves like a lossy dielectric at 10 GHz.

problems.title: Displacement current in a capacitor
problems.prompt: An air-filled parallel-plate capacitor ($A=1\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, $d=1\ \mathrm{mm}$) has $v(t)=10\sin(2\pi\times10^6t)\ \mathrm{V}$ across it. Find the displacement current between the plates and compare it with the current in the leads.
steps: It equals the conduction current in the leads exactly, so current is continuous around the circuit.

problems.title: Relaxation times
problems.prompt: Find the charge relaxation time of copper ($\sigma=5.8\times10^7\ \mathrm{S/m}$, $\varepsilon_r=1$) and of mica ($\sigma=10^{-15}\ \mathrm{S/m}$, $\varepsilon_r=6$).
steps: Charge put inside copper vanishes to the surface essentially instantly; charge on mica stays for hours.

problems.title: H from E with Faraday's law
problems.prompt: In free space, $\mathbf{E}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}\,10\cos(\omega t-\beta z)\ \mathrm{V/m}$ at $f=100\ \mathrm{MHz}$. Use Faraday's law to find $\mathbf{H}$, then check that it satisfies Ampère's law with $\mathbf{J}=0$.
hints: Only $\partial\tilde E_x/\partial z$ survives in the curl: it points along $\hat{\mathbf{y}}$.
steps: Check: $\nabla\times\tilde{\mathbf{H}}=-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\,\dfrac{\partial\tilde H_y}{\partial z}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}\,\dfrac{j\beta\,10}{\eta_0}e^{-j\beta z}$, and $j\omega\varepsilon_0\tilde{\mathbf{E}}=\hat{\mathbf{x}}\,j\omega\varepsilon_0\,10e^{-j\beta z}$. They match because $\beta/\eta_0=\omega\varepsilon_0$.
